# R0 — Editor’s + Author’s Prefaces (lines 122–196)

**Range read in full:** 122–196  
**Source:** Green, *The Gospel of Luke* (NICNT, 1997)

## Claims

### C1 — Series replacement of Geldenhuys; Fee as editor
**Locus:** 122–125 (slice ll. 1–4)  
**Quote:** "This replacement commentary (the eighth) represents another milestone for the New International Commentary on the New Testament, in that it replaces the first commentary to appear in the original series, that by Norval Geldenhuys in 1951."  
**Claim:** Green’s volume replaces Geldenhuys 1951; Fee situates it in NICNT evolution under Stonehouse → Bruce → Fee.

### C2 — Methodist/cross-confessional evangelical identity
**Locus:** 125–126 (slice ll. 5–6)  
**Quote:** "The present volume, the second in the series by a Methodist (along with I. Howard Marshall’s Johannine Epistles) is another indication of the cooperative, broadly based, cross-confessional dimension of the evangelical tradition…"  
**Claim:** Fee marks Green as Methodist; series goal remains thorough scholarship “loyal to Scripture as the infallible Word of God” (Stonehouse).

### C3 — Pastoral aim restored; narrative method vs atomistic Synoptics
**Locus:** 128–133 (slice ll. 8–12)  
**Quote:** "showing very little concern for traditional form-critical and redaction-critical issues… help the reader to see how the narrative “works,” how Luke’s own obvious concerns drive the narrative from beginning to end (including Acts)… without cross-referencing to Matthew or Mark."  
**Claim:** Fee commends Green’s post-form/redaction approach: read Luke on its own as continuous with Acts; primary audience pastors/teachers/students.

### C4 — Green’s institutional path (Fee)
**Locus:** 135–136 (slice ll. 14–15)  
**Quote:** "Ph.D. in New Testament in 1985 (from Aberdeen, Scotland)… New College (Berkeley) and the American Baptist Seminary of the West… As of the publication of this volume (Fall 1997) he begins his appointment as Professor of New Testament Interpretation at Asbury Theological Seminary… active pastoral life in the church."  
**Claim:** Aberdeen Ph.D. 1985; Berkeley teaching; Asbury appointment Fall 1997; pastoral engagement alongside scholarship. Dedication of volume timing: Holy Week 1997 (Author’s close).

### C5 — Green’s method pedigree: post-Conzelmann literary + social-scientific turn
**Locus:** 143–145 (slice ll. 24–26)  
**Quote:** "If the name of Hans Conzelmann is associated with the massive shift in Lukan studies… more recent exploration… Robert Tannehill and Luke Johnson on the literary side, and Halvor Moxnes and Philip Esler on the social-scientific… waning of the hegemony of historical study… blooming of so-called “newer” approaches…"  
**Claim:** Green locates his work after Conzelmann/Fitzmyer redaction era, aligned with Tannehill/Johnson narratively and Moxnes/Esler socially.

### C6 — Commentary vocation: whole-book, church-facing, multivalent Gospel
**Locus:** 145–147 (slice ll. 26–28)  
**Quote:** "those involved in the church’s ministry continue to be helped most by commentaries on whole books, written from the perspective of a fundamental reverence for the biblical text and from a position of critical engagement with academic biblical studies and active involvement in the life of the church… multivalency of the Gospel…"  
**Claim:** Green justifies commentary form for pastoral ministry; does not claim encyclopedic coverage of every possible question.

### C7 — CBA fellowship names method: discourse theory + sociological analysis
**Locus:** 149 (slice l. 30)  
**Quote:** "Catholic Biblical Association… Young Scholar’s Fellowship for my project “Toward a Unified Hermeneutic: The Application of Discourse Theory and Sociological Analysis to the Gospel of Luke” (1991–92)"  
**Claim:** Self-named project title equates his unified hermeneutic with discourse theory + sociological analysis (matches body “discourse analysis”).

### C8 — NRSV base text; limited text-criticism
**Locus:** 151 (slice l. 32)  
**Quote:** "I have chosen to employ the NRSV in this commentary. For the most part, I have refrained from discussing text-critical alternatives, though from time to time I have indicated in my editing of the NRSV where my own thinking departs…"  
**Claim:** NRSV is the running text; text-critical discussion is selective.

### C9 — Twelve interpretive asides listed (structural map)
**Locus:** 161–185 (slice ll. 41–65)  
**Claim:** Green flags twelve essay-like asides: birth structure; God’s purpose/Scriptures/beginning; social setting of 1:5–2:52; temple/incense; Magnificat; Benedictus; birth of Jesus literary/social; John’s prophetic ministry; 4:14–9:50 literary; Galilee region; faith and possessions; christology and discipleship in 9:1–50. Plus Figure 1 (Lenski power/privilege).

## Coverage
Read lines 122–196 complete. No body commentary in this range.
